definition: Text watermarking is a technique for embedding hidden information within textual content to verify its authenticity, origin, or ownership.
details: With the rise of generative AI systems using large language models (LLM), there has been significant development focused on watermarking AI-generated text. Potential applications include detecting fake news and academic cheating, and excluding AI-generated material from LLM training data. With LLMs the focus is on linguistic approaches that involve selecting words to form patterns within the text that can later be identified. The results of the first reported large-scale public deployment, a trial using Google's Gemini chatbot, appeared in October 2024: users across 20 million responses found watermarked and unwatermarked text to be of equal quality. Research on text watermarking began in 1997. Text watermarking has become a compliance tool as well as a research topic: under Article 50 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, applicable from 2 August 2026, providers of generative AI systems must mark their outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated, and China has required both explicit and implicit labelling of AI-generated content since September 2025. explainer.lead: Embedding hidden information in textual content to verify its authenticity, origin, or ownership. It matters as LLM-generated text spreads, with potential uses in detecting fake news and academic cheating and excluding AI-generated material from LLM training data.

tiers.eli5: It's like a hidden signature inside the words that lets someone later check where the text really came from.
tiers.practitioner: With LLMs the focus is on linguistic approaches that select words to form patterns identifiable later. Pitfall: the watermark only helps if the pattern can be reliably found after the text is edited or copied.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as embedding hidden information within textual content to verify authenticity, origin, or ownership. For LLMs the focus is on linguistic approaches selecting words to form later-identifiable patterns; the first reported large-scale public deployment was a triple.

explainer.example: An LLM chooses among candidate words so the output carries a detectable pattern, which a detector later uses to flag the text as AI-generated.
